analysis.one_liner: Requires court approval, independent monitoring, and public disclosure of corporate criminal settlements, and lengthens the deadline to prosecute corporate crime.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by a Democrat and a Republican, the bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in September 2024 and died there without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company commits a federal crime, prosecutors often settle with a deferred prosecution agreement: the company pays money and follows conditions, and the case never goes to trial. This bill would require a judge to approve any such deal with a corporation, weighing whether the penalty fits the offense and whether the company identified the people responsible. It would require federal agencies to post most settlement deals worth $1 million or more online, with the payment terms and how the money will be used; require independent, metrics-based compliance monitoring; extend the deadline for prosecuting corporate and financial-institution crimes from five years to ten; and block companies from getting reduced sentences unless they help identify the employees involved.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of corporate fraud and misconduct, shareholders, and the public, who today rarely see the terms of the deals prosecutors strike with large companies. A judge would check that penalties and admissions are adequate, the details of settlements of $1 million or more would be posted online for at least five years, prosecutors would have up to ten years to bring cases involving financial institutions or corporations, and companies could not earn lighter sentences without naming the employees responsible.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of corporate fraud and the public

how_it_helps.text: A court may not approve a deferred prosecution agreement with a corporation unless it finds the deal is in the public interest, weighing factors including the reasonableness of penalties, compliance safeguards, independent monitoring, and whether the company identified culpable individuals [S2].

Federal agencies must publicly post, in a searchable format, settlements (including deferred and non-prosecution agreements) of $1 million or more, listing the parties, the claims settled, each party's payment, how much is an actual penalty or is not tax-deductible, and where the money goes, and must post the agreement itself, kept up for at least five years (ten years for deals of $50 million or more) [S2].

Agencies must issue a public statement explaining why any confidentiality provision or sealing of a settlement is needed and why secrecy outweighs the public's interest, must break out penalty versus non-penalty amounts in public statements, and must report annually to Congress on settlement counts, confidential terms, attorney fees paid, and settlements involving regulatory changes [S2].

Corporations on probation or under compliance monitoring must employ independent monitoring using objective, methodologically sound metrics, and the Attorney General must report within one year on efforts to expand this practice [S2].
The deadline to prosecute a corporation or financial institution for an offense would extend from the general five-year window to ten years from the offense [S2].
A company seeking a reduced sentence for cooperation must provide assistance identifying and fully investigating the employees involved in the offense [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations and financial institutions that face federal criminal or civil enforcement would face bigger, court-reviewed penalties, longer exposure to prosecution, public disclosure of their settlement terms, independent monitors, and pressure to name responsible executives. Federal agencies and prosecutors would carry new reporting and disclosure duties, and companies would bear the cost of monitors and longer legal risk windows.

drawbacks.text: Requiring judicial approval of deferred prosecution agreements could make prosecutors more cautious about using them at all, potentially pushing cases to trial or leading prosecutors to decline weak cases, which could mean fewer accountability outcomes in practice [S2].

The disclosure mandate is limited: it applies only where information is not already covered by a confidentiality provision, so deals that agencies or companies agreed to keep secret could still stay hidden, though the agency head would have to publicly justify the secrecy [S2].

Extending the prosecution window to ten years increases legal uncertainty and defense costs for companies, and opponents of longer deadlines argue that evidence and memories degrade over time; companies would also bear the expense of independent compliance monitors [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency provisions are low-cost and address a real gap: the public currently often cannot see what large companies actually pay in settlements or how much is a true penalty versus a tax-deductible cost. Judicial review of corporate plea deals and a ten-year prosecution window are more intrusive changes whose effects depend on how courts and prosecutors implement them, and the confidentiality carve-out weakens the disclosure promise. On balance, the bill targets an accountability gap in corporate enforcement that costs victims and shareholders far more than the compliance burden costs companies.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late September 2024 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which took no action before the Congress ended, so it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Peter Welch (D-VT) introduced the bill on September 25, 2024, joined by Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO) as its sole cosponsor, making it a bipartisan pairing [S1] [S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S4].
No further action appears in the record: the committee never reported the bill, and it never reached the Senate floor before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations and financial institutions, which remain subject to prosecutor-negotiated corporate settlements without judicial review or mandatory public disclosure, and to the existing five-year prosecution window.

against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; it never received a hearing, markup, or committee vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat sponsored and a Republican cosponsored, but the bill drew only one cosponsor and no committee action, so it never developed a record of partisan division.

industries.note: The bill would subject corporate criminal settlements to judicial review, post their payment terms online, extend the prosecution window to ten years, and require companies to name responsible employees to earn lighter sentences. Their interest in negotiated, confidential, time-limited exposure runs against the public's interest in visible accountability.

The bill would require independent, metrics-based monitoring for corporate probation and deferred-prosecution deals, expanding demand for monitors whose role is to verify the company actually complies.
